To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) the matching relation is found in choice behavior between outcomes differing in the rate of food and the rate of shock; (b) the matching relation between food and shock is found in choice between outcomes differing in rate of food and rate of shock; and (c) the scale value of shock is equal in magnitude to that of food, though opposite in direction.

(1) the matching relation between choice and reinforcement rate holds for both positive and negative reinforcement and (2) the negative value of an aversive stimulus can be estimated by the amount of positive reinforcement that is necessary to offset the aversive stimulus.

(a) choice behavior is a function of the rate of reinforcement value of the outcomes, (b) the matching relation is obtained when outcomes are defined by the rate of reinforcement, and (c) outcomes are defined by a symmetrical law of reinforcement value.
In summary, our research is concerned with
a generalization of Herrnstein's (1961) matching law to include the effects of aversive stimuli.
a theoretical model of choice behavior that is derived from the symmetrical law of reinforcement effect.
the development of a functional theory of choice behavior that can be applied to both positive and aversive outcomes.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the symmetrical law of effects is a valid description of the choice behavior of the three pigeons tested.
the matching relation is a general principle of behavior, that the matching relation holds for choice between positive and negative reinforcers, and that the law of effect applies to choice behavior.

the matching relation between choice and rate of positive and negative outcomes is supported by the present results, as well as the majority of the literature on choice behavior in animals and humans.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

choice is determined by the rate of reinforcement value of the alternatives, with no special treatment given to the positive or aversive aspects of the outcomes. (Author/BL)
